The Missing Decision

A few words to know

A list used to find documents.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma read the final question in her notebook: Who checked that students received their decision letters? The trust's register had spaces for dates prepared and sent, but no place to record delivery.

The next morning, Fiona Bell emailed her a short page from an old office manual. It described what staff should do when a letter came back because the address was wrong. They should check the address, try to contact the student and make a note in the office records.

“Does this mean the trust followed up every letter?” Emma asked when Fiona called.

“No. It shows the instructions. I haven't found completed notes about returned letters.”

“Could the same instructions apply to letters that never came back, but never arrived?”

“I don't know. The page only mentions returned post.”

Emma called Sarah. They agreed that a missing receipt was not proof of a lost letter. The instructions were useful, but they did not show what had happened to any student.

“Can we look for a record of returned letters?” Sarah asked.

“That's the next question,” Emma said.

Emma sent Fiona a written request for a description of any records about returned post. She did not ask for students' names or addresses. While she waited, she checked the newspaper archive again.

The archive had not given her access to private letters. Instead, a member of staff offered to check whether an old index listed correspondence about the travel scheme. They warned that an index could describe a letter without showing what it said.

In the afternoon the archive sent one result. An entry from October 2011 described a letter under the subject “Student Travel — decision not received”. It did not include the writer's name or the letter itself.

Emma read the subject twice.

“That sounds like someone didn't get a decision,” Sarah said.

“It sounds like someone wrote about a missing decision. We haven't read the letter. We don't know what happened.”

“Could it be the parent who complained in September?”

“Possibly. But we have no evidence they're the same person.”

Emma added the entry to her notes, with the date and the archive's description. It was a lead, not a confirmed account.

At the end of the day, Fiona replied. The office manual did not mention sending reminders to students who had not replied. She was still checking for records of returned post.

Emma drew a line between two questions in her notebook. The first was whether the trust had tried to send decisions. The second was whether students could actually use their right to ask for a review.

A date in a register could not answer both.

She closed the laptop. Tomorrow, she would ask what the archive could verify about that October letter.
